q: What does this print? Type the two answers with a space between them.
code:
const { name, role = "guest" } = { name: "Ana", age: 30 };
console.log(name, role);
why: The pattern on the left matches by name. `name` is `"Ana"`. There is no `role` key, so the value is `undefined`, and the default `"guest"` is used.

q: Which of the three dots are rest, and which are spread?
options: `...nums` in the parameter list is rest. `...list` in the call is spread
`...nums` in the parameter list is spread. `...list` in the call is rest
why: Same three dots, opposite directions. On the left, in a pattern or a parameter list, the dots collect the leftovers (rest). On the right, in a call, an array or an object, they expand one value into pieces (spread).

q: What does the last line print?
why: Spread copies one level. It copies the arrow to the address object, not the object. Both outer objects share one inner object. Fix: spread every level you change.

q: Which of these are shallow copies, where the objects inside are still shared?
why: Spread and `Object.assign` copy the top level only. `structuredClone` copies every level.

options: `null`: a default is used only for `undefined`
why: `null` is a real value, so the default is not used. `0` and empty text are kept too. Use `??` when `null` should also get the fallback.

q: What does this print? Type the three answers with spaces between them.
why: `??` gives the fallback only for `null` and `undefined`, so `null ?? 10` is `10` and `0 ?? 10` keeps the `0`. `||` gives the fallback for anything that counts as false, so `0 || 10` is `10`.

options: An error, because the key is in both
why: A later key replaces an earlier one. The defaults came last, so your `size: 14` is lost. Fix: defaults first, your changes last: `{ ...defaults, ...mine }`.

q: `function show({ name }) { return name; }`. Calling `show()` with no argument gives `undefined`.
why: No. With no argument, the parameter is `undefined`, and you cannot unpack `undefined`. It throws a `TypeError`. Fix: give the whole parameter a default, `show({ name } = {})`.
No. The `= {}` default fills in only for `undefined`, like every default. `null` is a real value, so JavaScript tries to unpack it and throws a `TypeError`.

q: What does this print? Type the three answers with spaces between them. For the third, type the key names of `rest` joined together with no spaces.
why: `a` matches position 0, which holds `null`. `null` is not `undefined`, so the default `1` is not used. `b` has nothing at position 1, so its default `2` is used. `rest` collects the keys that were not named: `y` and `z`.

q: Put the steps of `const older = { ...user, age: 31 }` in the right order. `user` is `{ name: "Ana", age: 30 }`.
items: Then `age: 31` comes later, so it replaces `30`
`older` points at the new object, and `user.age` is still `30`
why: Spread only reads `user`. It builds a new object, and the original stays as it was.

q: Which of these use the three dots as rest, to collect?
why: Rest is on the left: in a parameter list or a pattern. It collects the leftovers into a new array or object, and it must be last. Spread is on the right: in a call, an array or an object.

q: `const { password, ...safeUser } = user;` gives a new object `safeUser` that has every field of `user` except `password`.
why: Rest collects every key that was not named into a new object. This is a common way to drop a field before you send an object out.
